title: Vitamin D, pre‐eclampsia, and preterm birth among pregnancies at high risk for pre‐eclampsia: an analysis of data from a low‐dose aspirin trial

sections.abstract: <jats:sec><jats:title>Objective</jats:title><jats:p>To examine the relation between maternal vitamin D status and risk of pre‐eclampsia and preterm birth in women at high risk for pre‐eclampsia.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Design</jats:title><jats:p>Analysis of prospectively collected data and blood samples from a trial of prenatal low‐dose aspirin.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Setting</jats:title><jats:p>Thirteen sites across the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">USA</jats:styled-content>.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Population</jats:title><jats:p>Women at high risk for pre‐eclampsia.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>We measured 25‐hydroxyvitamin D [25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D] concentrations in stored maternal serum samples drawn at 12–26 weeks’ gestation (<jats:italic>n</jats:italic> = 822). We used mixed effects models to examine the association between 25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D and risk of pre‐eclampsia and preterm birth, controlling for confounders including prepregnancy <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">BMI</jats:styled-content> and race.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Main outcome measures</jats:title><jats:p>Pre‐eclampsia and preterm birth.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>Twelve percent of women were vitamin D deficient [25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D <30 nmol/l]. Women with 25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D <30 versus ≥75 nmol/l had a 2.4‐fold (95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 1.0–5.6) higher risk of early‐onset pre‐eclampsia (<35 weeks’ gestation) after confounder adjustment. Women with 25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D <50 nmol/l had a 1.8‐fold (95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 1.0–3.2) increased risk of preterm birth at <35 weeks compared with women who had 25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D ≥75 nmol/l, which was driven by indicated preterm births at <35 weeks’ gestation [25(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OH</jats:styled-content>)D <50 versus ≥75 nmol/l adjusted <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> 2.5 (95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 1.1–5.8)]. There was no association between vitamin D status and pre‐eclampsia or preterm birth at <37 weeks.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title><jats:p>Maternal vitamin D status in the second trimester was inversely associated with risk of early‐onset pre‐eclampsia and preterm birth at <35 weeks in women at high risk for pre‐eclampsia.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Tweetable abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Vitamin D is inversely related to risk of pre‐eclampsia and preterm birth at <35 weeks in high‐risk pregnancies.</jats:p></jats:sec>
